prompt: Which device decides where a packet goes by reading its destination IP address?
hint: Layer 3 is the layer of IP addresses.

choices.text: A switch
choices.why: A switch reads the destination MAC address, at layer 2.

choices.text: A router
choices.why: Right. It reads the IP destination and picks the next neighbour.

choices.text: A hub
choices.why: A hub reads no address at all; it repeats the signal.

choices.text: An access point
choices.why: It bridges radio frames to the cable by their MAC addresses.

prompt: Match each device to what it reads before it decides.
hint: The deepest header each one looks at.
right_distractors: The name of the logged-in user

prompt: A box in a cupboard has 24 Ethernet ports. Frames between two of its ports are sent by destination MAC, and it has no IP address on either network it carries. What is it?
hint: Name it by what it reads, not by how many ports it has.

choices.text: A router, because it joins many machines
choices.why: A router reads IP and has an address on each network it joins.

choices.text: A hub with more ports
choices.why: A hub reads no MAC address; it repeats every bit to every port.

choices.text: A firewall
choices.why: A firewall judges addresses, ports and connections.

choices.text: A switch
choices.why: Right. Deciding by destination MAC is the switch's job, whatever the port count.

prompt: A switch learns which port a machine is on by reading the ___ MAC address of each frame that arrives.
hint: Not where the frame is going.

prompt: After pc1 pinged pc2, sw1's table held 02:25:70:bc:29:c6 on p1 and 02:fd:f2:d2:63:ba on p2. pc3 is cabled to p3 and its port is forwarding. Why is pc3 not in the table?
hint: Where does each entry come from?

choices.text: The table holds two entries at most
choices.why: It held three in a moment with three senders; the size is not the limit.

choices.text: pc3 has sent nothing yet
choices.why: Right. An entry is learnt from a frame's source, and pc3 has been silent since the table was emptied.

choices.text: pc3 is on a different network from pc1
choices.why: It is 10.20.10.23/24, the same network; and a switch reads no IP anyway.

choices.text: Port p3 is switched off
choices.why: bridge link show listed p3 as UP and forwarding.

prompt: pc3 ran tcpdump while pc1 pinged pc2 three times through sw1, and captured 0 packets. Why?
hint: Think about which cables the frames crossed.

choices.text: pc3's card threw the frames away because they were for pc2
choices.why: That is what a card does on a hub. Here the frames never reached pc3's cable.

choices.text: tcpdump ran without root
choices.why: It ran at a root prompt, root@pc3.

choices.text: sw1 knew both ports and sent nothing out of p3
choices.why: Right. With both MACs learnt, each frame left by one port.

choices.text: A switch does not carry ICMP
choices.why: A switch carries frames whatever is inside them; the pings worked.

prompt: sw1's forwarding database was empty. pc1 then pinged pc2 twice. How many dynamic entries did the table show afterwards?
hint: One per machine that sent something.

prompt: With the switch imitating a hub, pc1 pinged pc2 three times while pc3 listened. How many packets did pc3's tcpdump capture?
hint: Each ping is a request and a reply.

prompt: On the hub, pc3 showed frames from 02:25:70:bc:29:c6 to 02:fd:f2:d2:63:ba. Why did pc3's card keep frames addressed to another machine?
hint: What does tcpdump ask of the card?

choices.text: tcpdump put it in promiscuous mode
choices.why: Right. Without it, the card drops frames for other MACs; tcpdump asks it to keep them.

choices.text: The hub rewrote the destination to pc3's MAC
choices.why: A hub reads and writes no address; the capture shows pc2's MAC as destination.

choices.text: They were ARP broadcasts, which every card keeps
choices.why: The capture filtered icmp: these were echo requests and replies.

choices.text: pc3 and pc2 share one MAC address
choices.why: pc3 has its own; the frames named pc2's.

prompt: The lab set the bridge's ageing_time to 0 to imitate a hub. In what way is the result still NOT a real hub?
hint: A real hub works on the signal, not on frames.

choices.text: It still delivers every frame to pc3's port, whoever it is for
choices.why: That is the part the imitation gets right: pc3 caught 6 packets.

choices.text: It handles whole frames, both ways at once
choices.why: Right. A hub copies bits as they arrive, so a collision on one port reaches all of them.

choices.text: It reads the IP address in each frame before flooding
choices.why: Neither a bridge nor a hub reads IP.

choices.text: It has no ports
choices.why: It kept the same five ports.

prompt: From pc1, ping 10.20.10.10 answered with ttl=64 and ping 192.0.2.80 with ttl=62. What does the 62 tell you?
hint: Each router subtracts one.

choices.text: The answer took 62 milliseconds
choices.why: The time is the separate time= field; ttl is a counter.

choices.text: 192.0.2.80 is 62 hops away
choices.why: It started at 64 and lost one per router: the hop count is the difference.

choices.text: Two routers handled the reply
choices.why: Right. 64 minus 62: r1 and the provider, as traceroute confirmed.

choices.text: Two packets were lost
choices.why: 1 received, 0% packet loss: nothing was lost.

prompt: A Linux server answers a ping with a TTL that starts at 64. The reply crosses three routers on its way back. What ttl= does ping print?
hint: One per router.

prompt: The Linux setting that makes a machine pass packets from one interface to another is net.ipv4.___ = 1.
hint: sysctl printed it on r1.

prompt: Which of these does a router do that a switch does not? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of the TTL, broadcasts and unknown destinations.

choices.text: Stops a broadcast such as ARP's question
choices.why: Right. A broadcast stays inside its network.

choices.text: Floods a frame whose destination it has not learnt
choices.why: That is the switch's behaviour; a router discards what it has no route for.

choices.text: Subtracts one from the TTL of each packet it passes on
choices.why: Right. That is why ttl=62 counted two routers.

choices.text: Chooses the outgoing port by destination MAC
choices.why: That is the switch's decision, at layer 2.

choices.text: Has an address on each network it joins

prompt: What does an access point do with a Wi-Fi frame from a laptop?
hint: It sits between the radio and the cable.

choices.text: Gives the laptop an IP address
choices.why: That is the DHCP server's job, behind the access point.

choices.text: Turns it into the signal of the provider's line
choices.why: That is the modem, at the other edge of the building.

choices.text: Routes it to the internet by its IP address
choices.why: Routing is the router's job; the access point works at layers 1 and 2.

choices.text: Passes it on to the wired network, as a bridge
choices.why: Right. Radio on one side, Ethernet on the other.

prompt: Match each device inside a home provider's box to its job.
hint: Four devices, one case.

pairs.right: Turns the line's signal into Ethernet
Gives the home one public address
Provides the wired ports on the back

right_distractors: Picks a web server for each connection

prompt: Forty students in a lecture hall share one access point and Wi-Fi is slow, though its cable to the switch is fast and nearly idle. What explains it?
hint: Where is the shared part?

choices.text: The access point's MAC table is full
choices.why: It holds forty entries easily; the bottleneck is the air.

choices.text: The stations on one channel take turns on the same air
choices.why: Right. Like a hub's cable, one transmits at a time.

choices.text: The access point routes each phone on its own
choices.why: It bridges frames; it does not route.

choices.text: The cable is half duplex
choices.why: The cable is fast and idle, so it is not the limit.

prompt: pc1 fetched a page through r1. The 'established,related' counter went from 10 to 21 packets, and the 'eth0 to eth1' rule from 14 to 15. Why did the second grow by one?
hint: Which packet of a connection is new?

choices.text: The page was one packet long
choices.why: The first rule counted eleven more packets for the same exchange.

choices.text: The second rule counts bytes, not packets
choices.why: Both rules count packets and bytes.

choices.text: The firewall checks one packet in ten
choices.why: It checks every packet; the counters add up.

choices.text: Only the first packet opened a new connection
choices.why: Right. The rest, both ways, matched the established rule.

prompt: From the provider, curl -s -m 5 http://10.20.10.10/ printed nothing and then 'exit status 28'. What does that say about r1's rule?
hint: 28 is curl's code for a timeout.

choices.text: It dropped the packets and sent back no refusal
choices.why: Right. With drop the caller waits; reject would have answered at once.

choices.text: It rejected the connection immediately
choices.why: A rejection arrives at once; curl waited the full five seconds.

choices.text: It accepted it, but the server was down
choices.why: The drop counter rose to 5 packets: the firewall stopped them.

choices.text: It dropped 28 packets
choices.why: 28 is the exit status; the counter shows 5.

prompt: After the provider's attempt, how many packets had r1's last counter, 'everything else: dropped', counted?
hint: It was 0 before.

prompt: Put the lines of r1's forward chain in the order a packet meets them.
hint: The default comes when nothing else matched.
items: Accept what belongs to an established connection
Accept a new connection from eth0 out to eth1
trap: The policy is written at the top of the chain and applied at the bottom: it is what happens to a packet no rule took.

prompt: pc1's four requests to 192.0.2.80 were served by web2, web1, web2, web1. pc2's next request went to web2. What does pc2's result show?
hint: Whose counter is it?

choices.text: Each client starts its own sequence at web2
choices.why: Then pc1's earlier curl in the firewall test would not have got web1.

choices.text: One counter serves every client
choices.why: Right. numgen counts connections, so pc2 took the next turn.

choices.text: web1 was down for pc2
choices.why: It answered pc1 just before; there is no health check either way.

choices.text: pc2 is closer to web2
choices.why: The rule ignores where the client is.

prompt: web2 is switched off and lb keeps its rule, dnat to numgen inc mod 2. What do visitors to 192.0.2.80 see?
hint: Does the rule look at the servers?

choices.text: lb notices and sends every connection to web1
choices.why: That needs a health check, which this rule does not have.

choices.text: Every connection fails, to web1 as well
choices.why: web1 is still up and gets its turns.

choices.text: Half of the connections hang
choices.why: Right. Turns still alternate, and every second one goes to a machine that is not there.

choices.text: The router r1 drops them on the way
choices.why: r1 forwards them as before; the balancer chose the dead server.

prompt: Handing new connections to the servers in turn, one after another, is called round ___.
hint: Named after a petition signed in a circle.

prompt: A site must send requests for /api to one group of servers and pictures to another. What kind of balancer can do that?
hint: Where in the packet is the path /api written?

choices.text: A layer 4 balancer like lb
choices.why: It reads the address and port, and the path is inside the HTTP request.

choices.text: A layer 7 one
choices.why: Right. It reads the HTTP request itself.

choices.text: A router with one route per group
choices.why: A route is chosen by IP destination, and both requests go to 192.0.2.80.

choices.text: A switch with two ports
choices.why: A switch reads MAC addresses only.

prompt: Put the devices a request from pc1 to web1 crosses in order.
hint: Follow the office lab drawing from left to right.
trap: The balancer comes before the web server: the request is addressed to lb's 192.0.2.80, and lb chooses web1.

prompt: pc1 pings pc2 in the office lab. Which devices read the destination MAC address of pc1's frame? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which devices does the frame reach?

choices.text: sw1
choices.why: Right. It picks the port from it.

choices.text: pc2's network card
choices.why: Right. It keeps the frame because the MAC is its own.

choices.text: r1
choices.why: The frame stays in the office network and is never sent to r1's port.

choices.text: lb
choices.why: lb is two networks away; frames do not cross routers.

prompt: Match each thing seen in the lab to the device that caused it.
hint: One device per observation.

pairs.left: A different web server answered each time
A third PC captured another pair's pings
pairs.right: A hub, or a switch imitating one

pairs.left: A connection from outside timed out
The ttl of a reply was 62, not 64

prompt: A small company replaces its provider's all-in-one box with a separate modem, router, switch and access points. What does it gain?
hint: Think of placement, size and failures.

choices.text: Fewer IP addresses to manage
choices.why: The addressing plan does not depend on how many cases there are.

choices.text: A modem that also filters traffic
choices.why: Filtering is the firewall's job, on the router here.

choices.text: Each device sized, placed and replaced on its own
choices.why: Right. Access points go on ceilings, the switch in a rack, and one failure leaves the others working.

choices.text: No more need for NAT
choices.why: The router still shares the public address.
